family_basis: Select James Glasgow of the 1719 Dalziel record (Glasgow-3523) as John Glasgow-3094’s possible working father, at 41% subjective confidence. This joins the Cambusnethan John-and-Ann family provisionally to the adjacent Dalziel James-and-Samuel family. The positive comparison combines a particular nearby surname household, a viable parent generation, and John’s two currently listed sons James and Samuel repeating the older two given names. Samuel is a more discriminating comparison than John or James alone. The proposed sequence is Samuel to James to John to the later James and Samuel; only the first and last household roles have cited baptismal support. No record names the adult John’s father or shows the 1719 child’s later life. The 41% rates that whole immediate-father proposition, including the child-to-adult identity gap; it is comparative judgment, not a measured frequency or a probability for the complete pedigree.
limitations: John’s 1770 birth is an uncertain profile estimate, not a baptism or recorded age. If taken literally with 1719 it implies fatherhood at about 51, which is possible and supplies no maternity information. An illustrative John birth in 1750–1770 would give a James age of about 31–51 and a 1790 groom aged 20–40; neither range is adopted as a new date. The 15 March 1719 index date is not independently established as a birthday. The named James may have died young or belonged to another later household. Adjacency does not prove continuity, and an interval of roughly seventy years separates the two parish events. James and Samuel are the currently attached children, not a proved complete or birth-ordered family. Samuel could come from Ann Clerk’s family or another relative; no Scottish naming rule determines the father. The family names and the existing father assignment to Samuel are not independent demonstrations of John’s ancestry. Retain another local James or another unrepresented father, and a collateral relationship to the Dalziel family. Samuel Glasgow-3166 is an alternative direct father if John was substantially older than the 1770 estimate; the ordinary younger-groom generation favours an intervening James, but the absent age cannot exclude an older groom. The earlier Calder Alexander/Clerk-marriage comparison remains a possible wider ancestry route, not a proved direct father: repeated Clerk marriages do not identify Ann’s family or establish a two-century pedigree. Other Scottish James households are not excluded for missing fields, but no comparably specific Cambusnethan–Dalziel and James/Samuel sequence was found in the bounded local catalogue comparison. James’s mother and wife remain unknown. No mother is selected for John, and no relationship is inferred between Ann Clerk and the earlier Clerk women. Preserve the existing ungraded Samuel-to-James father mark and all current child-parent grades, without a confidence upgrade or live save. The 1690s–1794 London pen-cutter comparison for Samuel remains very weak and separate; it supplies no evidence for this family. No person is merged, created or redated.
